# PART A - EXAMPLES OF CONDITIONAL STATEMENTS

#### EXAMPLE A:
```{r}
score <- 78

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}
```

#### EXAMPLE B:
```{r}
score <- 86

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}
```

#### EXAMPLE C:
```{r}
scores <- c(92, 68, 75, 81, 59)
ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
```

#### EXAMPLE D:
```{r}
grade <- 91
attendance <- 95

if (grade >= 90 & attendance >= 90) {
  print("Honors candidate")
}
```

# PART B - CONDITIONAL STATEMENTS

**Question 1:**

- _Set temp <- 33. Print "Hot" if temp is 32 or higher, otherwise print "Not hot"_

*answer:*
```{r}
temp <- 33
if (temp >= 32) {
  print("Hot")
} else {
  print("Not hot")
}
# output: [1] "Hot" -> 33 is higher than 32 so the first block runs
```

**Question 2:**

- _Set age <- 17. Use if ... else if ... else to print "Child" for ages below 13, "Teenager" for 13 to 19, and "Adult" for 20 and above._

*answer:* 
```{r}
age <- 17
if (age < 13) {
  print("Child")
} else if (age <= 19) {
  print("Teenager")
} else {
  print("Adult")
}
# output: [1] "Teenager" -> 17 is not below 13, but it is 19 or less, so the second condition is TRUE
```

**Question 3:**

- _Create marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62). Use ifelse() to create a vector result that says "Pass" for marks of 60 or higher and "Fail" otherwise. Print result._

*answer:*
```{r}
marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
print(result)
# output: [1] "Fail" "Pass" "Pass" "Pass" "Pass"
# only 45 is below 60, so it is the only Fail
```

**Question 4:**

- _Predict the output of the code below before you run it. Then run it and explain, in a comment, why you got that result._
```{r}
# x <- 10
# if (x > 5) {
#   print("A")
# } else if (x > 8) {
#   print("B")
# } else {
#   print("C")
# }
```

*answer:*
```{r}
x <- 10
if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C")
}
# I predicted "A" and the output was [1] "A".
# Why: R reads the conditions from top to bottom and stops once one is TRUE.
# x > 5 is already TRUE for 10, so it prints "A". The x > 8 part is also TRUE
# but R never gets to it.
```

**Question 5:**

- _What is the difference between if and ifelse()? When would you choose each one?_

*answer:* if checks a single condition and runs a block of code, so it suits one value and control flow (e.g. deciding what to do next). ifelse() checks every element of a vector at once and returns a vector of results, so it suits creating or transforming a column of data, like the Pass/Fail vector in Question 3.

### f.Applying Conditional Statements

- _f.1. Compute the final grade.** Any arithmetic with NA gives NA, so the student with the missing midterm will have NA as a final grade. This is expected._

*answer:*
```{r}
# weighted grade: quiz 30%, midterm 30%, final 40%
grades$FinalGrade <- 0.30 * grades$Quiz + 0.30 * grades$Midterm + 0.40 * grades$Final
```

- _f.2. Pass or fail.** Check for NA first, because NA >= 75 gives NA, not TRUE or FALSE._

*answer:*
```{r}
# the inner ifelse only runs for students with a grade, NA goes to "Incomplete" first
grades$Result <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                 ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed"))
```

- _f.3. Grade remarks.** Replace each *blank* with the correct cutoff or label, then change eval=FALSE to eval=TRUE in the chunk header._

*answer:*
```{r}
# nested ifelse: NA first, then the cutoffs from highest (90) down to lowest (75)
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 90, "Excellent",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85, "Very Good",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 80, "Good",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Fair", "Needs Improvement")))))

# anything below 75 that is not NA ends up as "Needs Improvement"
```

- _f.4. Attendance flag.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column AttendanceFlag with "At Risk" when Attendance is below 80 and "OK" otherwise._

*answer:* 
```{r}
# below 80 attendance is At Risk, everything else is OK
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
```

- _f.5. Honors candidates.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column Honors with "Yes" or "No". Use & to require both a final grade of 90 or higher and attendance of 90 or higher. Students with a missing final grade must get "No". Hint: use !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) as the first condition._

*answer:* 
```{r}
# !is.na() goes first so the student with no final grade becomes "No"
# & means both conditions (grade and attendance) must be TRUE
grades$Honors <- ifelse(!is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 90 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Yes", "No")
```


- _f.6. if ... else if inside a loop.** ifelse() works on a whole column, but a plain if handles one value at a time. To use if on a column you must loop over the rows._

*answer:*
```{r}
# i is the row number, so each loop checks one student only
for (i in 1:nrow(grades)) {
  if (is.na(grades$FinalGrade[i])) {
    print(paste(grades$Name[i], "- Incomplete"))
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 90) {
    print(paste(grades$Name[i], "- Excellent"))
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 85) {
    print(paste(grades$Name[i], "- Very Good"))
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 80) {
    print(paste(grades$Name[i], "- Good"))
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 75) {
    print(paste(grades$Name[i], "- Fair"))
  } else {
    print(paste(grades$Name[i], "- Needs Improvement"))
  }
}
```

- _f.7. Now try if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") on its own in the Console. Explain the error or warning R gives and why the loop version avoids it._

*answer:*
```{r, eval = FALSE}
if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed")

# In R 4.2 and newer this gives the error "the condition has length > 1".
# Older versions only gave a warning and used the first value.
# The reason is that if needs just one TRUE or FALSE, but grades$FinalGrade >= 75
# gives 15 values (one per student).
# The loop works because grades$FinalGrade[i] is only one value at a time.
```

- _f.8. Summarize your results.** Then write in comments how many students passed, how many are At Risk, and how many are honors candidates. Compare with a seatmate._

*answer:*
```{r}
sum(grades$Result == "Passed", na.rm = TRUE)
sum(grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk")
sum(grades$Honors == "Yes")

# na.rm = TRUE on the first one so the NA (Bea) is skipped instead of breaking the sum
# My results:
# Passed: 10 students
# At Risk: 4 students (Mark Villanueva, Jenny Bautista, Carlo Mendoza, Daniel Flores)
# Honors candidates: 4 students (Maria Santos, Kristine Lopez, Liza Ramos, Sofia Domingo)
```

- _f.9. Check grades should now have 12 columns (7 original plus FinalGrade, Result, Remarks, AttendanceFlag, Honors)._

*answer:*
```{r}
ncol(grades) == 12
```

# PART D - EXPORTING RESULTS TO .CSV

**Question 7:**

- _a. Export the full processed table.** The argument row.names = FALSE stops R from adding an extra numbering column._

*answer:*
```{r}
write.csv(grades, "students_grades_processed.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

- _b. Export the at-risk students.** The file is written only when there is at least one at-risk student._

*answer:*
```{r}
at_risk <- grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]
if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}
```

- _c. Export the honors list._

*answer:*
```{r}
# the part before the comma picks the rows (Honors is "Yes"),
# the part after the comma picks the 5 columns I want to keep

honors <- grades[grades$Honors == "Yes", c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")]
# only export if there is at least 1 row, if not just print a message
if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  print("No honors candidates.")
}
```

- _d. Verify your exports. Never assume a file was written correctly. Read it back and compare._

*answer:*
```{r}
# read the saved file back to see if it matches the original data
check <- read.csv("students_grades_processed.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dim(check) == dim(grades)      # same number of rows and columns?
all.equal(check, grades)       # same values too?
head(check)

read.csv("at_risk_students.csv")
read.csv("honors_list.csv")
```

**Question 9:**

- _a. Add a column Scholarship to grades using these rules, then export the qualified students._

*answer:* 
```{r}
# grades$Scholarship <- "None"
# grades$Scholarship[!is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90] <- "Partial"
# grades$Scholarship[!is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90] <- "Full"
```

- _b. Use nested ifelse() statements. Test the missing grade first, then Full, then Partial_

*answer:*
```{r}
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Pending",
                      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
                      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial", "None")))
```

- _c. Select students whose Scholarship is "Full" or "Partial". Hint: %in% c("Full", "Partial")._

*answer:*

```{r}
scholars <- grades[grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"), ]
```

- _d. Export them to scholarship_candidates.csv with row.names = FALSE, using an if ... else guard._

```{r}
if (nrow(scholars) > 0) {

} else {

}
```

**Question 10:**
```{r}
# 1. Why did you check is.na() before comparing the final grade to a number?
# 2. In Task 3.2, what would happen if the Failed condition were placed before the Incomplete condition?
# 3. When is ifelse() the better choice than if ... else, and when is if ... else better?
# 4. Why is it useful to read an exported CSV back into R?
```

*answer:*
```{r}
# 1. NA >= 75 gives NA instead of TRUE or FALSE, so the code can get messed up.
#    I had to deal with the missing grade first.
# 2. Bea's NA would go through the Failed test first and give NA, so she would never be marked "Incomplete".
# 3. ifelse() is better when I need to check a whole column or vector at once.
#    if ... else is better for one value, or for things like checking if a file exists before using it.
# 4. To make sure the file was saved right (correct rows, columns and values) before I submit or send it.
```
